title: Approve chapter 1 of The Last Signal

result.title: The Frequency
result.content_text:
The cold came in through the gaps in the tower wall the way it always did, not all at once, but in fingers, finding the places where Mara had stuffed rags between the corrugated panels and working around them with patient, seven-year persistence. She woke to it at four in the morning by the wind-up clock she kept on the floor beside her cot, its luminous hands the color of old teeth.

She lay still for a moment, listening.

The tower groaned. Below her, the water tank that had given the structure its purpose sat empty and rust-scoured, a forty-thousand-gallon drum that now served mainly as an echo chamber for the wind. Above her, the catwalk she'd reinforced with salvaged angle iron held her weight and her equipment and not much else. The whole structure leaned three degrees to the northwest, which she'd measured with a plumb line on the day she moved in and had tried not to think about since.

She sat up. Her sleeping bag, military surplus, the synthetic fill gone flat in patches from years of compression, fell away from her shoulders and the cold finished the job the wind had started. She pulled on her jacket without standing, a practiced motion, then her boots, lacing them in the dark by feel alone.

The receiver was where it always was. She didn't need light to find it.

The console had been a broadcast board once, the kind that sat in the production room of a regional AM station, she knew because she'd stripped one herself, before the Pulse, for a public radio affiliate in Salina, Kansas, during a renovation. This one she'd found in pieces in the rubble of a strip mall in what had been Abilene, spread across three rooms as if someone had tried to move it and given up. She'd carried it out in a canvas duffel over four trips, walking four miles each way, and spent eleven days rebuilding it on the catwalk with a soldering iron run off a car battery and a manual she'd memorized so thoroughly she no longer needed to open it.

It was not beautiful. The front panel was buckled along the left side where something heavy had struck it, and she'd replaced two of the fader knobs with wooden dowels she'd whittled herself, sanded until they moved smoothly in the channels. But the receiver section worked. That was the thing that mattered. That was the only thing.

She switched it on.

The hiss that filled her headphones was the sound she'd been waking to for seven years, and she had never once gotten used to it. Not because it was unpleasant, she'd made her peace with that, but because it was alive. The static on the HF bands was not silence dressed up as noise. It was the atmosphere itself, breathing: lightning from a storm system three thousand miles away cracking through the spectrum like a dry branch, the sun's own magnetic weather pressing down on the ionosphere and warping the long-wave paths in ways she could feel in her fingertips before she could name them. The cosmos was broadcasting. It had always been broadcasting. The Pulse had only turned off the human voices that had made it hard to hear.

She swept the dial from the low end of the 40-meter band upward, the way she did every morning, moving in increments of ten kilohertz and pausing at each stop for a count of fifteen. It was a discipline she'd given herself in the first year, when she'd still believed she would find something, another station, a military frequency, a voice, and had kept after she'd stopped believing, because the discipline itself was the point. You maintained the practice or you lost the skill. You lost the skill and you were just a woman living in a broken tower with a box of wires.

At 7.200 megahertz she paused longer than usual.

There was something in the static there. Not a voice. Not even a tone. Just a texture, a density to the noise that was slightly wrong, the way a shadow on a wall is slightly wrong when it doesn't match the object casting it. She adjusted the fine-tune capacitor, a quarter-turn left, and listened.

Nothing resolved. The texture dissolved back into undifferentiated hiss.

She moved on.

By the time she reached the top of the 20-meter band the sky outside the tower's single intact window had begun to pale from black to the color of a bruise. She could see, in that thin light, the shape of the town below her: the collapsed storefronts along what had been Main Street, their facades caved inward like faces with broken noses; the grid of streets that still held their geometry even with the asphalt heaved and cracked by seven summers of freeze-thaw cycles; the water tower's shadow, long and tilted, reaching northeast across the rubble like an accusatory finger.

She'd chosen this town, Garfield, population eight hundred and twelve, according to a sign she'd found under a drift of topsoil, because it was small enough to be empty and high enough above the surrounding plain that her antenna wire, strung from the tower's crown to a fence post forty meters away, cleared the worst of the ground-level interference. She'd chosen the tower because the height gave her a better radiation angle for skywave propagation. She'd told herself these were the only reasons.

The other reason was that it was far enough from Crale's nearest settlement that no one came through without a purpose.

She poured water from the thermos she'd filled the night before, barely warm now, tasting of the copper pipe she'd run from the rain catchment, and drank it standing up, still wearing her headphones, one ear cocked to the receiver. Outside, something moved in the rubble below. She went still.

A dog. Three-legged, its coat the color of old concrete, picking its way along the base of the tower with the deliberate economy of an animal that had learned not to waste a step. It stopped, looked up at her through the window with yellow eyes, then moved on.

She let out the breath she'd been holding.

Seven years, and she still tensed at a dog.

She set down the thermos and wrote the morning's log entry in her notebook, a composition book she'd waterproofed by rubbing the cover with rendered fat, its pages dense with her small, precise handwriting. *0412. Sweep 7.0, 14.35 MHz. Atmospheric noise elevated, consistent with active ionosphere. No structured transmissions. Solar flux index estimated high by propagation character. Anomaly at 7.200, possible interference artifact, could not resolve. Will revisit at 0600.*

She underlined *anomaly* and then, after a moment, underlined it again.

The clock on her workbench read 05:47 when the signal came.

She almost missed it. She'd been on the 40-meter band for twenty minutes, parked at 7.200 again, and the texture she'd noted at 0412 had returned, that same slight wrongness in the static, like a word spoken in another room that you can't quite make out but can't stop listening for. She'd been about to move on. Her hand was already on the dial.

Then: three tones.

Clean. Spaced. Rising in pitch, not a random harmonic, not a lightning artifact, not the kind of accidental resonance that a long-wire antenna could generate from a nearby metal structure. Three distinct tones, each held for approximately one second, each separated by a half-second of silence. She knew the difference between noise that sounded like a pattern and a pattern that sounded like noise. This was the second thing.

She did not move.

A pause. She counted in her head. Four seconds, maybe five.

Then five tones. The same structure, the same pitch spacing, but five of them, and the last one held a fraction longer than the others, the way a sentence holds its final syllable when the speaker wants you to understand that it is not finished.

Another pause. Longer this time, she counted eight seconds, and then a burst of what she could only call chaos: a rapid, uneven stream of dits and dahs that tumbled over each other like stones down a slope. Corrupted Morse. The timing was wrong, the spacing between characters irregular, the whole burst lasting perhaps twelve seconds before it cut off and the static swallowed it whole.

Mara did not breathe until the static had been unbroken for thirty seconds.

Then she pressed rewind on the cassette deck, a battered Marantz she'd hardwired into the receiver's output, running off a separate battery, loaded with a tape she'd been using and erasing and reusing for two years, and played it back.

Three tones. Pause. Five tones. Pause. Twelve seconds of corrupted Morse.

She played it again.

On the third pass she picked up her pencil and began to transcribe. She drew a horizontal line across the notebook page and marked it in one-second intervals, then placed the tones above it as vertical bars, short ones for the half-second gaps, taller ones for the tones themselves. It was a method she'd developed in the first year, when she'd still been trying to decode the ghost signals that turned out to be reflections of old broadcast infrastructure, metal towers resonating in the wind at their own harmonic frequencies. She called the method a timing diagram, though she'd never told anyone that, because naming it made it feel more real than she wanted it to be.

The structure was immediately clear on paper in a way it hadn't been in her ears. The three tones were evenly spaced. The five tones were evenly spaced. The interval between the two groups was consistent. This was not drift. This was not artifact. This was a clock, something was keeping time at the other end of this transmission.

She sat with that for a moment.

Then she turned to the Morse burst and began the slower work.

The problem with corrupted Morse is that it doesn't corrupt evenly. The timing drifts, a dit that should last one unit stretches to one and a half, a dah that should last three compresses to two, and the spaces between characters collapse or expand in ways that make word boundaries impossible to read on a single pass. But the shapes of the characters themselves, the underlying rhythm of each symbol, tend to survive. A skilled ear can reconstruct probable characters from probable rhythms the way a reader can reconstruct a word from a smudged page. You don't read every letter. You read enough.

She played the burst six more times.

By the fourth pass she had four candidate characters written in her notebook, each with a question mark beside it. By the sixth pass she'd resolved two of the question marks. She was left with something that looked like: *F, E, ?, A*

She stared at it.

The pencil was still in her hand. She became aware that she'd been pressing it against the page hard enough to score the paper beneath.

*F. E. A.*

Not a word. Not a call sign. A fragment, the kind of fragment you got when a transmission was cut short, or when the encoding was damaged, or when the sender was working with equipment that was failing. She'd seen fragments like this before. She'd spent a year cataloguing them before she'd accepted that cataloguing fragments was not the same as understanding them.

But there was something else. Something about the three-tone, five-tone structure that had been sitting at the back of her mind since the first pass and that she'd been refusing to look at directly, the way you refuse to look directly at something you've seen in your peripheral vision because looking at it directly will confirm that it's real.

She pulled the timing diagram toward her and measured the intervals with her thumbnail against the page.

Three tones. 1.0 seconds each. 0.5-second gaps between them.

Five tones. Same.

The gap between the groups: 4.0 seconds, give or take the imprecision of her counting.

She set the pencil down.

The FEMA Emergency Broadcast Protocol, the one she'd spent eight months helping to draft in the two years before the Pulse, sitting in a conference room in a federal building in Kansas City with three engineers and a lawyer who kept asking whether the tones needed to be patented, used a framing sequence of exactly this structure. Three attention tones, a four-second pause, five confirmation tones. The sequence was designed to be unmistakable on a degraded channel. It was designed to survive noise. It was designed to be recognized by someone who knew what they were listening for, even if everything that followed it was garbage.

She had argued, in that conference room, that the five-tone confirmation was redundant. The lawyer had agreed with her. She'd been overruled by the senior engineer, a man named Holt who wore his gray hair in a flat-top and drank his coffee black and had spent thirty years in emergency communications and had very little patience for people who thought redundancy was waste.

*Redundancy is not waste,* Holt had said. *Redundancy is the only reason anything works when everything is failing.*

She had written that down. She still had it, in a notebook she'd carried out of Kansas City in the first week after the Pulse, one of eleven notebooks she'd packed before she'd packed food.

She looked at the timing diagram.

Three tones. Four-second pause. Five tones.

Holt's sequence.

Her sequence.

She stood up from the workbench so fast that her stool tipped and clattered against the tower's concrete floor, and she stood there in the middle of the room with the headphones still around her neck and the playback still running, static, just static now, and she thought: *No.*

No. Because the protocol had never been fully deployed. Because the bunkers that were supposed to use it had been decommissioned, or converted, or simply never built. Because she had helped write a protocol for a system that had not existed in any complete form when the Pulse hit, which meant that anyone transmitting this sequence was either working from a document they'd found, a training manual, a draft specification, or they had been inside the room where it was written.

Or they were broadcasting a coincidence.

She picked up the stool. She set it back in place. She sat down.

She played the tape again.

*Three tones. Pause. Five tones. Pause. Corrupted Morse.*

She wrote in her notebook, underneath the timing diagram and the four candidate characters: *Coincidence. Equipment artifact. Ghost signal, old transmitter cycling on residual power. Atmospheric reflection of a pre-collapse test broadcast.*

She underlined each one. Then she wrote: *FEMA EBP framing sequence, confirmed structure.*

She did not underline that.

She looked at the four characters again. *F, E, ?, A.*

The middle character, the one she hadn't been able to resolve, had a rhythm she'd been reading as a dah-dit-dah. Which would make it K. But the timing was compressed, which could collapse a dah-dit-dit into something that sounded like dah-dit-dah. Which would make it D.

*F, E, K, A.* Or *F, E, D, A.*

She wrote both versions. Then she wrote, in smaller letters beneath them: *Grid fragment?*

Federal emergency grid references, the ones used in the operations manuals she'd seen in Kansas City, were alphanumeric, four to six characters, structured to identify a regional sector within a larger coordinate system. Four characters was a partial reference. Enough to tell you which region. Not enough to tell you where in it.

She looked at the window. The sky outside was the color of old pewter now, the sun still below the horizon but the darkness thinning. The water tower's shadow had shortened since she'd last looked.

She should eat something. She should check the antenna connections, which she hadn't done since the wind three days ago. She should write this up properly and then set it aside and wait, wait for the next transmission, if there was one, and the one after that, and see whether the pattern held.

She should not sit here with her hands flat on the workbench and her heart doing something she didn't have a name for.

She picked up her pencil and drew a box around *F, E, ?, A.*

Then she tore the page out of the notebook.

She held it for a moment, the timing diagram, the candidate characters, the boxed fragment, and she thought about the stove in the corner, which she kept burning low through the night for warmth and which would take this page without effort, without residue, without consequence.

She thought about Holt, who was almost certainly dead.

She thought about the lawyer, whose name she had never remembered.

She folded the page once and set it on the workbench, under the corner of the receiver, where it would not blow away.

The Morse burst had lasted eleven seconds.

She knew this because she had counted it four times on the tape, marking each repetition in the margin of her notebook with a small vertical line, the way she used to mark signal events in the old log sheets at the station, a habit so old it had become reflex, her hand moving before her mind caught up. Eleven seconds. The framing sequence accounted for the first seven. That left four seconds of content, which at standard Morse speed gave her perhaps eight to twelve characters, depending on spacing. She had recovered four with any confidence. The rest was noise eating signal, the static's appetite greater than the transmission's strength.

She spread her notes on the workbench and looked at what she had.

The timing diagram took up most of the page, a row of long and short marks she'd drawn while listening, her pencil pressing harder than she'd meant to, the dashes thick and the dots barely there. Beneath it, the candidate characters. Beneath those, the two versions of the grid fragment: *FEKA* and *FEDA*. Beneath those, in her own handwriting, the list of explanations she'd written to explain it away.

She picked up the list.

*Coincidence.* She read the word aloud, quietly, to see how it sounded. It sounded like a word she'd used before. It sounded like the thing she'd told Dov, six months ago, when she'd picked up a faint carrier wave on 7.2 megahertz and spent three days trying to resolve it into something before the frequency went dead. *Probably a coincidence,* she'd said. *Old transmitter running on a corroded battery somewhere, cycling until it stopped.* Dov had nodded and traded her four D-cells for the company and never asked about it again.

That had been a coincidence. She was fairly sure of that. The carrier had been unmodulated, no structure, no content, just a tone fading in and out with the ionosphere's daily shift, the way a dead channel breathed.

This was not unmodulated.

She set the list down.

*Equipment artifact.* She looked at the receiver. It was a Realistic DX-394, scavenged from a ham operator's estate sale, the ham had died in the second winter, of cold and then of pneumonia, and his widow had traded the radio for two months of firewood before she'd understood what she had. Mara had carried it forty miles on her back, wrapped in her sleeping bag, and she had been maintaining it ever since with the focused anxiety of someone who knows that the thing she is caring for cannot be replaced. She knew every quirk of it. The squelch control that stuck at the low end. The slight drift in the digital readout that she corrected by ear. The way the AGC circuit sometimes pumped on strong static bursts, making a noise that sounded almost like a rhythm.

Almost. Not like this. Not with four-second pauses timed to the tenth of a second.

She crossed out *Equipment artifact.*

*Ghost signal, old transmitter cycling on residual power.* She'd seen this twice in seven years. Both times the signal had been on AM broadcast frequencies, and both times it had been a simple carrier, no modulation, no structure. A transmitter running on the last of a backup battery, broadcasting nothing into the dark. The framing sequence required a functioning digital controller or a very precise human operator. A ghost transmitter didn't have either.

She crossed that out too.

*Atmospheric reflection of a pre-collapse test broadcast.* She almost didn't cross this one out. Ionospheric reflection was real, HF signals bounced off the F-layer and came back down hundreds of miles from their source, sometimes thousands. On the right frequency, at the right time of night, you could hear things from very far away. She had heard, once, what she was nearly certain was a Spanish-language broadcast from somewhere south of the border, a man's voice, reading numbers in a flat cadence, the kind of numbers-station format that had been popular with intelligence services before the Pulse. She'd never been able to confirm it. She'd written it down and moved on.

But a pre-collapse test broadcast would have been recorded. Recorded signals didn't drift in the way this one had, the slight timing compression in the middle character, the noise floor rising and falling with the transmission as if the source power was fluctuating. A recording played back through a transmitter held its timing. A live operator, or a live digital controller running on marginal power, did not.

She crossed it out.

That left the line she hadn't underlined.

*FEMA EBP framing sequence, confirmed structure.*

She looked at it for a long time. Outside, a bird called once, something small, a sparrow or a wren, the kind of bird that had come back faster than anything else because it needed so little. She heard it land on the antenna wire, the faint elastic twang of the wire taking the weight, and then nothing.

The Emergency Broadcast Protocol had been a working group project. She'd been brought in because of her background in signal processing, specifically her work on noise-resistant tone encoding for low-power transmitters. The working group had met four times over eight months, in a conference room in a federal building in Kansas City that smelled of carpet cleaner and old coffee, and they had produced a forty-seven-page specification document that had been submitted to the relevant office and then, as far as she had ever known, shelved.

Shelved. Not implemented. Not deployed.

She pressed her thumb against the edge of her notebook until the skin went white. Here was the thing she kept coming back to, the thing that made her want to put the page in the stove: the protocol had never been deployed. Which meant that whoever was transmitting it had access to the specification. Which meant they had either found a copy of the document, possible, the document existed, she had a copy herself, folded into the back of the third notebook she'd packed, or they had been in the working group.

There had been seven people in the working group. Holt. The lawyer. Three engineers, two of whom she'd barely known. A FEMA regional coordinator who had attended only the first and last sessions and had spent both of them on his phone. And her.

Seven people. Seven years. She did not know where any of them were.

She picked up the page with the timing diagram and held it between her fingers. The paper was the back of a seed catalog, the kind that had been printed by the millions and now served as the wasteland's most reliable writing material, blank on one side, pictures of tomatoes and squash on the other. She'd written her notes on the blank side. If she turned it over she'd see a photograph of a beefsteak tomato, improbably red, with a caption that said *Best Flavor, Guaranteed.*

She didn't turn it over.

The stove was three steps away. She could see the orange line of heat around the door's edge, the iron warm enough that the air above it shimmered slightly. The page would go in two seconds. The notes would be ash in five. She would close her notebook and eat something and go check the antenna connections and wait for the next transmission, which would probably not come, because ghost signals did not repeat with new content and equipment artifacts did not evolve and ionospheric reflections did not carry grid fragments.

She stood up.

She took one step toward the stove.

The receiver spoke.

Not static. Not the broadband hiss she'd been living inside for seven years, the white noise that had become so familiar she heard its absence as silence. This was narrow. Focused. The same frequency, 7.455 megahertz, the same slight carrier hum she'd logged at 0312. The framing sequence began without preamble, three tones, clean as struck glass, and then the four-second pause, and then five tones, and then the Morse.

Different Morse.

She crossed the room in two steps, dropped into the stool, pulled the headphones over her ears with hands that were not entirely steady, and pressed the record button on the tape machine before she'd consciously decided to. Her pencil was already moving. The signal was stronger this time, not much, but enough that the noise floor dropped away from the characters like mud washing off stone, and she could hear the spacing clearly, the dits and dahs arriving with a precision that made the first transmission seem ragged by comparison.

She wrote what she heard.

When the burst ended, nine seconds, this time, she counted without thinking, she sat with her pencil on the paper and looked at what she'd written.

Six characters. Clean. No ambiguity in any of them.

*3, 8, N, 1, 0, 4.*

She knew what that was before she'd finished writing it. She knew it the way she knew the framing sequence, not from memory she'd had to work for, but from the kind of deep-grooved recognition that lives below thought, in the part of the mind that does not argue.

38 North. 104 West.

Latitude and longitude, abbreviated to the degree. No minutes, no seconds, not yet. But 38 North, 104 West put you in a box roughly two hundred miles on a side, straddling the Colorado-Kansas border, high plains and scrubland and the eastern edge of the Rockies. She had driven through that box once, years before the Pulse, on a road trip she barely remembered. Flat land, brown grass, the mountains a blue suggestion to the west.

Somewhere in that box, someone was transmitting on a frequency she had helped design a protocol for, using a framing sequence she had helped write, sending coordinates in a format that matched federal emergency operations standards.

She looked at the page in her hand. The timing diagram. The four candidate characters from the first transmission. The stove, three steps away, its door edged in orange.

She set the page down on the workbench. She set the new page next to it. She looked at both of them together, the partial fragment from the first transmission, the cleaner coordinates from the second, and she felt something shift in her chest, a sensation she recognized distantly as the feeling of a decision being made in a place she didn't have direct access to, the decision arriving finished before she'd had a chance to argue against it.

She was not going to burn the notes.

She was also not, she told herself, going to do anything else. Not yet. She was going to wait for the third transmission, if there was one. She was going to verify the pattern. She was going to be careful and methodical and she was going to write everything down and she was not going to think about what 38 North, 104 West meant, or who was there, or how far it was, or whether they were still alive.

She picked up her pencil.

In the margin of the new page, in letters small enough that she could pretend she hadn't written them, she wrote: *~400 miles.*

The stove ticked as the iron cooled. She hadn't fed it.

She sat with both pages on the workbench in front of her and did what she always did when she didn't trust herself: she checked her work.

The framing sequence first. Three tones, pause, five tones, she'd logged the inter-tone spacing at 1.1 seconds on the first transmission, 1.08 on the second. Close enough that the difference was drift, not design. The carrier frequency: 7.455 megahertz on both. She pulled the logbook from under the bench, a hardbound ledger she'd scavenged from a collapsed accountant's office, its pre-collapse columns still faintly visible beneath her penciled entries, and checked the atmospheric notes she'd made at 0200. The ionosphere had been quiet. No lightning signatures in the HF bands, no solar noise spikes. Whatever she'd heard, she hadn't heard it because the sky was misbehaving.

She wrote that down too, in the margin, in the same small letters.

Then she looked at the six characters again.

*3, 8, N, 1, 0, 4.*

The format nagged at her. Not the coordinates themselves, those were plain enough, degrees only, a box drawn around the high plains. What nagged was the encoding. She'd heard emergency coordinates transmitted in Morse before the Pulse, during drills, during the two weeks after the Pulse when some of the hardened government stations had still been broadcasting. They'd used decimal notation. Degrees, decimal minutes, full precision. Four significant figures after the decimal point, minimum. The format was in the protocol documentation she'd helped draft in 2019, sitting in a conference room in Kansas City with three FEMA comms officers and a styrofoam cup of bad coffee, arguing about whether to standardize on MGRS or stick with lat-long.

They'd stuck with lat-long.

But they'd never used abbreviated degrees-only. That wasn't the protocol. Degrees-only was a truncation, a shorthand, the kind of thing you used when you were rationing something. Bandwidth, maybe. Or power.

She got up and went to the shelf above the window where she kept the manuals.

Most of them were technical: ARRL handbooks, FCC frequency allocations, a battered copy of *Emergency Communications for Amateur Radio* that she'd read so many times the spine had given up. But at the far end, wedged between a diesel engine repair guide and a water purification manual, was a thinner volume, a FEMA internal document she'd been given at the end of the Kansas City meeting and had kept because she kept everything. The cover read *FECC Comms Annex C: Degraded-Environment Transmission Standards*, and someone had stamped it *DRAFT, NOT FOR DISTRIBUTION* in red ink that had faded to pink.

She hadn't opened it in seven years. She hadn't needed to. She'd been part of the conversation that produced it.

She brought it to the bench and opened it.

The pages smelled of the particular damp that came from paper stored near an exterior wall through multiple winters, a cold, faintly sweet rot that she associated now with the preserved and the lost in equal measure. She found the section she wanted on page 31. *Annex C-7: Coordinate Transmission Under Power-Constrained Conditions.*

She read it standing up, one hand flat on the page.

Under power-constrained conditions, defined as available transmission power below fifteen percent of rated output, operators were authorized to transmit coordinates in abbreviated format: degrees only, cardinal direction, no decimal extension. The receiving station was expected to acknowledge and request refinement in subsequent exchanges. The logic was simple: get the rough location out first. Precision could follow if the power held.

Below fifteen percent.

She looked at the receiver. The needle on the signal-strength meter had barely moved off the noise floor on either transmission. Whoever was sending this was not broadcasting from a well-fed station. They were trickling power into an antenna and hoping someone was listening on exactly the right frequency at exactly the right time.

She closed the manual and set it on top of the two pages of notes.

Outside, the wind had come up. She could hear it working at the gap in the south wall she'd packed with rags last autumn, a thin, persistent whistle that rose and fell without settling. The stove had gone quiet. The room was colder than she'd noticed.

She pulled her coat from the hook by the door, canvas, military surplus, the kind that had been everywhere in the first years after the Pulse when the army depots were still being picked over, and put it on without taking her eyes off the bench.

Degrees only. Power-constrained. The framing sequence from a protocol she'd helped write. A format from an annex she'd helped draft and then forgotten about because the world had ended before anyone had needed to use it.

She thought about the conference room in Kansas City. The styrofoam cup. The FEMA officer across the table, a woman named Garrett, or Garrety, she couldn't remember, who had argued for MGRS on the grounds that it was what the military used and they should standardize on the people with the guns. Mara had argued for lat-long on the grounds that civilians would need to read these coordinates off paper maps, and paper maps used lat-long, and the point of emergency communications was to be understood by people who were scared and tired and possibly untrained.

She had won that argument.

She wondered if Garrett-or-Garrety was alive. She wondered if anyone else from that room was alive. She wondered if the person on the other end of 7.455 megahertz had been in that room or had only read the document afterward, had found the annex in some hardened facility's filing system and followed it because it was the procedure and following procedure was what you did when everything else had stopped working.

She picked up her pencil. On a fresh page, the back of what had been a grocery circular, a photograph of a whole roasted chicken visible through the paper when she held it to the light, she began a new column.

At the top she wrote: *What I know.*

Below that: *7.455 MHz. Framing sequence per FECC protocol. Annex C-7 abbreviated coordinates. Two transmissions, 41 minutes apart. Signal strength: marginal. Power-constrained sender.*

She drew a line under that and wrote: *What I don't know.*

She looked at the second column for a long time. Then she wrote: *Everything else.*

The wind found the gap in the south wall again and the whistle climbed a half-step, held, dropped. Somewhere outside, one of the loose antenna guy-wires tapped against the exterior boards in a rhythm that was almost, but not quite, regular.

She looked at the receiver.

The needle sat on the noise floor, motionless.

She looked at the clock on the shelf, a wind-up mechanical, the only kind that still worked reliably, its face scratched but its hands steady. 0501. The sky outside the east-facing window was still black, but the black had thinned at the horizon to something closer to charcoal. In an hour it would be grey. In two it would be light enough to work outside.

She thought: if there is a third transmission, it will tell me something. The minutes, maybe. The seconds. Enough to narrow the box.

She thought: if there is no third transmission, I have two pages of notes and a draft annex and a coordinate that puts me somewhere in a two-hundred-mile square, and that is nothing, that is less than nothing, that is the kind of thing that gets people killed, moving toward a vague location on the strength of a signal that came twice and stopped.

She thought: forty-one minutes between the first and the second.

She looked at the clock again. 0502.

She sat down on the stool, pulled the headphones back over her ears, and set her pencil on the fresh page.

She would wait until 0543. If nothing came, she would close the notebook and go outside and check the antenna connections and eat something and decide later, in daylight, with a clear head, what any of this meant.

She pressed her fingertips against the headphone cups and listened to the static breathe.

She waited until 0544 before she admitted nothing was coming.

She took the headphones off slowly, as if the signal might still be there if she moved carefully enough. It wasn't. The static breathed on without her.

She looked at the two pages of notes. Then she did something she hadn't done since the first winter after the Pulse, when she'd found a cache of blank index cards in a collapsed stationery shop and felt briefly, absurdly rich: she tore the page into thirds.

Not to destroy it. To copy it.

She worked by the lamp, her handwriting smaller than usual, more deliberate. The coordinate fragment first, the four characters, exactly as she'd decoded them, no interpretation, just the raw groups. Then the framing sequence. Then the frequency and the two timestamps. She copied it three times onto three separate scraps, checking each one against the original before she set it aside. When she was done she had three identical records on three different pieces of paper.

She folded two of them. The first she tucked into the spine of the ARRL handbook on the second shelf, the one she'd carried for four years and never lent to anyone, which meant it was the safest place in the building for something small. The second she rolled tight and pushed into the gap in the wall behind the stove, behind the rags, where the wind came through in winter. Cold back there, and damp, and anyone who searched the room would look at the shelves and the bench and the floorboards and not at the packing in the wall.

The third she kept in her hand.

She sat with it on the stool for a while, not reading it. She already knew what it said.

The lamp was burning lower, the oil was nearly gone, and she'd been running it since before midnight. In the thinning light the bench looked different. Smaller. The receiver sat where it always sat, its needle on the noise floor, its dials exactly where she'd left them. The two pages of notes lay beside the closed manual. Everything in the room was the same as it had been eight hours ago.

Nothing in the room was the same as it had been eight hours ago.

She picked up the pencil. She opened the log, the actual log, the one she kept in the sewn-paper notebook she'd been filling for two years, the one that recorded frequencies monitored, atmospheric conditions, antenna adjustments, battery levels, anything she heard that was worth noting. Most entries were three lines. A date, a frequency, a remark. *Possible voice fragment, 14.225, could not verify. Lightning interference, south bearing, 0300, 0600. Antenna connection corroded, replaced with scavenged copper, signal improved 2 dB estimated.*

She found the current page. At the top she had written yesterday's date and a note about the barometric reading and the condition of the long-wire antenna after last week's wind.

Below that she wrote four words.

*It is not noise.*

She set the pencil down.

The wind found the gap in the south wall and the whistle climbed and held and dropped. The loose guy-wire tapped the exterior boards. Outside, the horizon had gone from charcoal to a dull, flat grey that was not yet light but was no longer dark, the colour the sky turned when it was deciding.

She looked at the four words.

Someone had built a transmitter. Someone had maintained it for long enough to know what frequency to use and what protocol to follow and how to structure a coordinate in the abbreviated MGRS format from Annex C-7, which was not a document that circulated widely, which was not something you found by accident. Someone had waited, weeks, months, she didn't know, for the power reserves to reach a level that justified the draw. Someone had keyed a transmitter in the dark and sent three tones and a pause and five tones and a pause and then a burst of corrupted Morse that contained, inside the corruption, four characters that meant something.

And then they had sent it again, forty-one minutes later, because that was what the protocol said you did. You sent twice and you waited. You acknowledged the possibility that no one was listening. You sent anyway.

She thought about what it took to do that. To keep sending into silence for, how long? Six months, Amara had written, or someone had written, or the signal implied. Six months of transmissions that had reached no one, or had reached people who didn't know what they were hearing, or had reached people who knew and chose not to answer. Six months of keying the transmitter and waiting and hearing nothing back and keying it again.

She thought about what kind of person did that.

She thought about what kind of person was still alive underground, seven years after the Pulse, in a facility with power reserves measured in percentages and a transmitter that barely moved the needle off the noise floor.

Twenty-three people, she thought, and then stopped, because she didn't know that. She didn't know anything. She had four characters and two timestamps and a framing sequence, and she was already building a story around them the way you built a fire, the smallest possible materials, arranged carefully, hoping for heat.

She looked at the scrap of paper in her hand.

The four characters were a fragment of a grid reference. She knew the format. She'd argued for a different format in a conference room in Kansas City and lost, and so she knew this one too, because knowing the formats you'd argued against was part of the job. Four characters placed you in a hundred-kilometre square. You needed six for ten kilometres. Eight for one kilometre. Ten for a hundred metres.

She had four.

She had a box two hundred miles across.

She thought: that is not enough to move on. That is not enough to tell anyone. That is not enough to do anything with except sit here and wait for the next transmission and hope it carries the next two characters, and then the next two after that, and then you would have a location, a real location, something you could put a finger on a map and say *here.*

She thought: there might not be a next transmission. The power reserves might have dropped below the threshold. The transmitter might have failed. The person sending might have, she did not finish that thought.

She thought: there is no one else within four hundred miles who can read this.

She had not meant to think that. It arrived without permission, flat and certain, the way true things arrived. She sat with it.

She knew the frequencies. She knew the protocols. She had spent seven years maintaining a receiver and a log and a set of skills that the wasteland had no obvious use for, that she had maintained out of habit or stubbornness or the particular kind of grief that expresses itself as *I will not stop doing the thing I was good at.* She had listened to static for seven years. She had written down everything she heard. She had kept the antenna connections clean and the receiver calibrated and the log current, and she had told herself it was discipline, it was practice, it was what you did when you didn't know what else to do.

And now someone was transmitting on 7.455 megahertz using a protocol she had helped write, and she was the only person in four hundred miles who knew what it meant.

She folded the scrap of paper and held it between her palms.

The lamp guttered. The oil was gone. The room went dim, lit now only by the grey light coming through the east window, thin and flat, enough to see by but not enough to make anything look like itself. The receiver sat in the half-dark. The needle sat on the noise floor.

She thought: I should sleep.

She thought: I should eat something.

She thought: I should go outside and check the antenna connections and decide later, in daylight, with a clear head.

She did not move.

The four words were still in the log. *It is not noise.* She looked at them and thought about what they meant, not as a technical conclusion but as a fact about the world, about the specific world that existed right now, this morning, in the hour before full light, seven years after everything had stopped.

Someone was alive. Underground. Transmitting.

And waiting.

She unfolded the scrap of paper and looked at the four characters again. Then she turned to a fresh page in the log, drew a rough outline of the region from memory, the kind of sketch she'd made a hundred times, the river courses and the ridge lines and the old highway corridors, and placed a circle on it, large and imprecise, centred on nothing she could yet name.

She stared at the circle.

Somewhere inside it, a transmitter was running on reserves that might not last another week. Somewhere inside it, someone had followed a protocol from a document that had been written in a conference room she remembered, on a day she remembered, when the world had still been the kind of place where you wrote protocols for emergencies you hoped would never happen.

The emergency had happened. The protocol had survived. Someone was using it.

She closed the log.

She sat in the grey light with the scrap of paper in her hand and the circle on the map and the four words written down, and she understood, with the particular clarity that comes at the end of a sleepless night when you have stopped arguing with yourself, that she was not going to decide later.

She had already decided.

The question, the one she hadn't written down, the one that sat under everything else like a frequency she hadn't tuned to yet, was whether whoever was sending the signal had any idea what they were transmitting into. Whether they knew what the wasteland had become. Whether they knew about Crale.

She thought: they don't know.

She thought: someone has to tell them.

Outside, the sky had made up its mind. The grey had gone pale at the edges, and the first thin light was coming in flat across the bench, across the receiver, across the two pages of notes and the closed manual and the log. The loose guy-wire had stopped tapping. The wind had dropped.

In the new silence, the receiver's needle sat exactly where it had always sat.

She kept watching it anyway.
